newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Bardot tells all - for the love of animals.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bardot tells all - for the love of animals.

text.p: Brigitte Bardot, the former sex symbol who was known to the world simply as B.B., is about to reveal all.
The sultry French film star who held a generation of men in thrall is to publish her memoirs on October 1, days after her 62nd birthday.
In them she tells of her experiences in the cinema, which gave her world fame and which she loathes, and of the men she loved and who drove her to solitude and desperation.
"B.B., that's over. Don't speak to me about cinema any more. I wrote what I had to say. Full stop," she told the weekly Paris Match.
But to read what she has to say, fans must wait for the book itself, "Initiales B.B.". Eager to maximise the income for her animal rights foundation, she has banned publication of any excerpts.

Bardot made her film debut at 18 in "And God Created Woman", the film by her husband Roger Vadim which propelled her to instant fame. Her stunning pout, long blonde hair and sexy curves were envied and copied by hundreds of thousands of women and plunged an army of male worshippers into "Bardolatry".

Her early films helped brush away the cobwebs of sexual inhibition in many countries. For a generation of Frenchmen, she became a national treasure -- also called the country's top export -- combining the pride, the passion and the special magic of France itself.
Sculptor Alain Gourdain-Aslan took her as his model for "Marianne," the symbolic figure of the French Republic whose bust is found in every town hall in the country.

She made the last of her 46 films 18 years later and declared the cinema world to be "rotten," retiring as a secretive recluse in the fashionable Riviera resort of Saint- Tropez with a menagerie of cats and dogs.
Her secluded seaside villa, La Madrague, was for a time a focus of attraction for paparazzi and fans eager to catch a glimpse of the sad and lonely figure sunning herself.
Then the fascination dimmed and Bardot was heard of only through her passionate outbursts in defence of animals -- seals against hunters, bulls against bullfighters, sheep against Moslem revellers.
By her own admission, the sad truth behind the glitter was that her private life was a mess of broken marriages, shattered love and disenchanted solitude.

On her 26th birthday she was found unconscious at a Riviera house after a suicide attempt. She mysteriously cancelled her 49th birthday party and appeared later in hospital, triggering rumours of another suicide bid.

Bardot started writing "Initiales B.B." the day after her 40th birthday, during a period of depression. The result, 22 years later, was 1,500 pages, handwritten with her "whole heart, head, soul and guts...total truth, absolute sincerity".
"It was sometimes a very painful experience. But I think that it also saved me at times from immense desperation," she told Paris Match in an interview giving glimpses of her book.
Despite repudiating her life as a star, Bardot could not resist repeating for the magazine's photographer some of her most famous, 35-year-old poses.
She writes of the men she loved and who left her, of her co-stars. Her first husband, Vadim, "remains like my elder brother, a wonderful friend", she said.
Her second husband, actor Jacques Charrier, the father of her only child Nicolas, scared her. "Our relationship was difficult, violent...We would quarrel and fall in each other's arms".
Playboy and business heir Gunther Sachs was the only man who left a deep mark on her. "I could have stayed with him, but fate decided otherwise," she said.
With French rebel singer Serge Gainsbourg, it was "mad love, dream love".
"I had a deep-rooted need to be loved...to belong soul and body to a man I admire, love and respect," she said.
Alain Delon? Bardot the animal lover cannot forgive him for promoting fur. "He gets on my nerves, always showing off his blue eyes...But he is a monument, a monument with blue eyes."

Besides frustration, cinema gave Bardot money and fame, the tools for a second life. In 1987 she auctioned off a wealth of personal souvenirs to raise funds for an animal protection organisation, the Brigitte Bardot Foundation.
"Fame was the only valuable thing cinema brought me. Fame allows me to fight for a cause which is not only that of the animals but that of the weak against the strong," she said.
Demonstrating, firing statements at the press, she defends Alaskan wolves against aircraft-assisted hunting, dogs against South Korean gourmets, pigeons against French hunters.

She took on Russian President Boris Yeltsin for failing to stop the butchering of reindeer and Sophia Loren for lending her name to the promotion of fur coats. She campaigned to have the late president Francois Mitterrand abolish the French presidential hunting grounds.
She faced death threats for urging a ban on horsemeat and confronted game hunters who held a congress in Saint-Tropez.
Bardot, who married right-winger Bernard d'Ormale in 1992, ran into trouble from human rights groups for an outburst against Moslem immigrants in France earlier this year.
"France, my homeland, my land, is...again invaded by a foreign, especially Moslem overpopulation...We see mosques flourish while our church bells fall silent," she wrote then.
She later explained she was protesting only against the ritual slaughter of sheep for the Aid-el-Kebir Moslem feast.
